name: anti-corruption-layer
intent: Protect a downstream bounded context from a foreign model by making one explicitly owned boundary translate calls, data and failure semantics into the downstream language; unlike a mere wrapper, an anti-corruption layer prevents foreign concepts from becoming domain concepts.
problem: A bounded context must use a legacy application, packaged product, partner API or another context whose model it cannot control, and the same words carry different meanings on each side. Reusing the foreign SDK types and status codes directly makes its names, optionality, units, errors and version churn load-bearing parts of the local domain; translation then drifts across callers and every upstream change becomes a core-model change. Without an explicit boundary, the contexts become accidental conformists and neither can evolve independently.
context: Use it at a durable integration seam where the models genuinely disagree and at least one side cannot be changed: a new core beside a legacy or packaged system, a core subdomain consuming a third-party service, two bounded contexts with different vocabularies, or a staged migration whose callers must survive a callee replacement. It is a boundary-scoped investment: a model worth protecting must exist on the downstream side, and the seam must be durable enough to own a component; a wire-level rename, a CRUD screen over a stable API or throwaway code does not justify it.
benefits: The downstream model stays in its own language: foreign terms, structures and idioms are translated once at the seam, so the domain keeps one coherent vocabulary instead of a mixture of yours and theirs.
The upstream cannot dictate your design: its types, naming, quirks and version churn stop at the boundary, so new requirements are shaped by the domain, not by what the legacy model happens to offer.
Both sides evolve independently - an upstream version change, a protocol switch or a migration step becomes an edit inside the layer instead of a coordinated change across the domain.

Boundary concerns get one home: validation and sanitisation of untrusted payloads, protocol mechanics, authentication, timeouts, retries, circuit breaking, correlation and tracing live in the layer instead of being scattered through domain code.

Testability improves on both sides: the domain is exercised against its own port with a fake or in-memory adapter, and the translation itself is pure mapping code testable with captured upstream payloads, without the upstream being available.
Incremental migration becomes possible: because callers keep talking to the seam, functionality can move from the old system to the new one one slice at a time while both keep working.

The relationship between the two models is made explicit: an anti-corruption layer documents that two contexts genuinely differ, which is more honest than presuming a shared language nobody maintains.
tradeoffs: Two models to maintain: every foreign concept you care about gets a local counterpart, so the mapping code and the DTO/domain duplication must be kept in sync deliberately - drift here is silent data corruption, not a compile error.

An extra hop and an extra copy: translation adds latency and allocation on every call, and in high-load paths the layer itself can become the scaling bottleneck unless it is sized with the dependency it fronts.

The layer is a new failure and operations surface: it must be deployed, configured, monitored and supported like any critical component, and it becomes a single point of failure for everything behind it.

Translation is lossy and asymmetric: information the local model does not represent (or the upstream cannot express) is dropped or smuggled outside the model, and those corners have to be decided and documented rather than discovered in production.

Scope creep is structural: the layer is the natural place to 'just add' orchestration, caching, business rules and deserialisation shortcuts, which turns it into a second, unowned domain model - the corruption it was built to prevent.

It tends to become permanent: an anti-corruption layer introduced for a migration outlives the migration unless it is tracked as technical debt with an explicit decommission criterion, leaving a boundary nobody dares to remove.

It protects only what is inside it: the boundary holds because the rest of the code respects the module rules, and one bypassing call path reintroduces exactly the coupling the layer was meant to prevent.

participants.responsibility: The bounded context whose model is the asset being protected; it speaks only its own language, calls the layer's port, and never addresses the upstream system directly.
The boundary component (module, assembly or service) that owns the seam: the only code that knows both models, and the only permitted path to the upstream.

The interface the domain calls, expressed entirely in downstream terms - a facade for a use case or a set of ports for capabilities; the domain can be built and tested against it with no upstream in sight.
Implements the port against the upstream interface: converts calls and arguments, invokes the upstream, returns results for translation - and carries no domain rules of its own.

Converts models in both directions: field and structure mapping, unit, date and encoding conversion, value normalisation, invariant checks, and translation of upstream errors and status codes into the downstream error vocabulary.

The upstream-protocol client inside the layer (HTTP client, database driver, RPC/SOAP stub, event consumer): it owns transport, authentication, correlation, timeouts and resilience policy, and its types never leave the layer.

use_cases: Staged migration (strangler style): a monolith keeps calling a capability that has been extracted into a service, and the layer converts the old call into the new semantics so existing callers are not modified while functionality moves out piece by piece.
Legacy or packaged systems: an ERP, mainframe, CRM or vendor database with convoluted schemas and obsolete protocols is consumed by a new core domain that refuses to adopt its concepts.
Third-party services inside a core subdomain: a payment, identity or logistics API whose model must not shape your domain — its statuses, optionality and error codes are mapped to your own types.

Two bounded contexts in one product: the upstream team publishes a model your context rejects (conformist would be too costly), so your side translates it and the context map records the relationship.
Event-driven integration: upstream events are translated, validated and re-emitted as downstream domain events before any handler in the core sees them.
Standardised external formats: EDI, ISO 20022, FHIR or partner schemas are parsed into a local model inside the layer, keeping the standard's vocabulary out of the domain.
Replacing an infrastructure dependency: swapping the persistence engine, message broker or identity provider behind a layer while the domain keeps exactly the same vocabulary.

Database-view ACL for analytics: a database view that maps another context's internal storage schema into an analytics-owned projection, used instead of direct cross-context SQL queries that couple the analytics context to the source's implementation details.

API-gateway-level ACL: an Azure Functions, AWS Lambda or similar serverless function deployed at the API gateway seam that performs domain-model translation before requests reach the downstream service, keeping protocol handling and semantic translation separate.

Dark launch / shadow traffic validation: an ACL running in parallel that receives mirrored traffic and logs translation discrepancies without affecting live callers, enabling validation of a new integration before any traffic is cut over.

Multi-system data aggregation: a domain that must compose data from multiple external systems with incompatible models (e.g., a customer dashboard pulling from Stripe, Salesforce and an on-premises ERP) translates each system's model separately before assembling a unified view.

Bidirectional payment provider integration: a payment gateway ACL that translates inbound webhooks (provider → local domain events) and outbound charge requests (local domain → provider format), with a stable provider-independent reference as the operation key on every call.

Legacy system read-through cache: an ACL that wraps a legacy system's slow query with asynchronous cache warming and model translation, so the domain sees a fast, semantically correct response without coupling to the legacy's latency profile.

AWS Migration Hub Refactor Spaces strangler migration: Amazon API Gateway routes a monolith's calls to legacy or Lambda services while an ACL converts the monolith's old interface to the migrated service and is removed after callers move.

Spring Boot customer integration: a Spring component with an external client, explicit mapper, retry policy and circuit breaker translates provider responses into local aggregates; keep the ACL inside the service unless several consumers need the same boundary.

Azure Strangler Fig migration: an Azure façade routes legacy and new services while a domain-owned ACL translates calls in both directions, letting clients keep the same interface until the legacy feature is retired.
avoid_when: The upstream semantics are compatible and you own both sides: conform to one shared model, or consume an intentionally shared Published Language, instead of paying for a translation layer that copies an identical model.

The difference is only a field rename, wire format or method signature: use a Message Translator, DTO mapper or Adapter (serde, Jackson, Codable, struct tags) - an ACL is for incompatible meanings, not interface-shape compatibility.
There is no downstream model to protect (CRUD screens, transaction script, thin reporting): a direct client with a data mapper is the simpler and more honest structure.
The integration is genuinely throwaway, or the feature is scheduled for deletion: write the small adapter now rather than a boundary you must maintain and then decommission.

The upstream is already fronted by a component that owns its semantics (a service the upstream team maintains for you, an SDK with deliberate domain types), so a second translation would duplicate an existing contract.
The foreign data is infrastructure data that never enters the domain model (telemetry, logs, metrics): a plain client library is enough.
The need is routing, authentication, rate limiting or protocol termination: use a generic API gateway; it is not an ACL unless it also owns semantic translation for a downstream model.
The upstream deliberately offers an Open Host Service for many consumers: use its stable protocol or negotiate an extension instead of wrapping an intentionally shared contract in a private ACL.
Both contexts agree to communicate through a documented Published Language such as FIX or ISO 20022: translate at each context's edge and do not mistake the shared language itself for an ACL.
anti_patterns: Leaky boundary: expose upstream types, ids or raw payloads; the domain imports the foreign model anyway, so return local types and keep foreign values private.
Rule creep: add business rules, orchestration or compensation to the ACL; it becomes an unowned second domain model, so keep policy in domain services.
Bypass path: allow one 'temporary' direct call beside the ACL; two models and failure behaviours then diverge, so enforce one dependency path.
God ACL: share one layer across unrelated external systems; one release or outage couples every integration, so keep boundaries service-specific.
Blind mapping: use reflection or name matching across fields; unit, encoding, null and ordering differences silently corrupt data, so map semantic fields explicitly.
Zombie migration scaffolding: keep an interim ACL after cutover; it becomes unowned and stale, so track a decommission trigger and remove it when callers migrate.
Facade-only ACL: rename the upstream SDK without translating its model; the structure of the pattern remains but foreign semantics still leak, so design the port from local concepts outward.
design_principles: Boundary and information hiding: the foreign model is an implementation detail of one component; nothing outside it may depend on upstream types, ids or errors.
Dependency inversion: the downstream domain owns the port it calls; the adapter depends on the domain's vocabulary, never the other way round.
Separation of concerns: translation is not domain logic - the layer maps models, transports and errors, and does nothing else.
Single responsibility per role: facade, adapter, translator and gateway change for different reasons and should be separable.
Explicit context mapping: naming the relationship between two models, and its direction, is part of the architecture and not an accident of a shared database.
Fitness functions over good intentions: enforce the boundary with dependency rules, import checks or module tests, because architecture by convention erodes under deadline pressure.
best_practices: Design the port first, in downstream terms: write the interface your domain wishes existed and then make the adapter satisfy it — never shape the port after the upstream API.
Keep translation pure and total: dedicated mapping functions with explicit cases for missing, optional and out-of-range values, and no reflection-style blind property copying where semantics differ.
Translate errors and statuses explicitly: map upstream exceptions, codes and partial failures into the downstream error vocabulary, and decide at the boundary whether a failure is retryable.

Put resilience and observability in the gateway: timeouts on every call, bounded retries only for idempotent operations, circuit breaking for overloaded upstreams, correlation ids and translation-failure metrics.
Validate and sanitise at the seam: the layer is the trust boundary for untrusted payloads, so schema validation and normalisation belong there, before domain code ever sees data.
Enforce the boundary mechanically: dependency rules, import checks or a test that fails when upstream packages appear outside the layer, plus reviewer attention to 'just this once' direct calls.
Version and test the mapping against the upstream: contract tests or captured golden payloads per upstream version, so a silent upstream change fails a test instead of corrupting the model.
Decide the layer's lifecycle up front: permanent boundary or migration scaffold? If the latter, record it as technical debt with a decommission trigger and monitor whether it is still needed.
Keep it thin and service-specific: one layer for one upstream (or one cohesive group), with no caching or orchestration beyond what the boundary itself needs.

Use contract tests for translation fidelity: capture real upstream responses as golden-payload test fixtures and verify the translator produces the expected downstream model — catch integration drift before it reaches production.

Treat unknown and unmapped values explicitly: when an upstream field has no mapping, throw a descriptive error or produce a clearly-tagged union result — silent defaulting hides data-quality defects that surface at runtime.

Monitor translation failure rates and boundary latency: alert on spikes in translation errors, unmapped field counts and latency regressions — the ACL is where upstream changes break first and visibility is critical.

Prefer stable provider-independent references as operation keys: use a plain string reference agreed with the upstream rather than their internal ID type, so the adapter can be swapped without changing domain call sites.

Version translation mapping tables explicitly: when the upstream changes a field name or enum value, record the mapping version in the payload audit trail so regressions are traceable and rollback is possible.
Separate ACL from orchestration: the layer translates models and manages transport — business rules, multi-step coordination and compensation logic belong in domain services, not in the translator.

Measure your 'corruption score': search for external system field names, enum values and type references inside your domain classes — every hit is work an ACL would have saved, and the count justifies the investment.

pitfalls: Letting the adapter return upstream types or raw maps 'for now': the domain then depends on the foreign model even though the layer exists; external types that cross the boundary make every downstream caller a leakage point.

Scattering translation through the codebase: field access, unit conversion and status mapping outside the boundary give the foreign model a second home and make every future upstream change a multi-file edit.
Growing the layer into an application service: orchestration, caching and domain rules make it a second, unowned domain model — the corruption it was built to prevent has simply moved house.
No enforcement of the boundary: without a module dependency rule, an import check or a CI test that fails on foreign imports, the boundary decays one call site at a time under deadline pressure.
Treating the layer as free: forgetting timeouts, retries and error translation makes the upstream's failure semantics the domain's problem, and the layer becomes an uncaught exception source.

Leaky abstraction: the ACL wraps but does not translate — exposing external types (Stripe.Charge, legacy enums) directly in its return shape; the domain still depends on the foreign model and the layer is structural only.

Bidirectional coupling: changes in the downstream domain require changes to the external system, or vice versa, because the port was shaped after the upstream API rather than designed from the domain outward.

Missing error translation: external exceptions, error codes and partial failures propagate untranslated into the domain, scattering 'catch AxiosError' blocks throughout domain code instead of centralising them at the seam.

Incomplete translation testing: the adapter is tested only with hand-crafted happy-path data; null values, unknown enum codes, malformed payloads and boundary values are never exercised, and those are exactly where translation bugs hide.

Performance bottleneck: the ACL becomes the single scaling choke point for all traffic to an upstream dependency because it was not sized or designed with the upstream's throughput characteristics in mind.

God ACL (shared layer for all integrations): one shared ACL for every external system couples unrelated integrations into a single release train and failure domain, so one team's change affects all consumers simultaneously.

Blind mapping: reflection-based field copying or name-matching serialisation that silently ignores unit, encoding, null and ordering differences between the models, producing wrong answers without any error signal.

Zombie migration scaffolding: an interim ACL kept after the migration finished — unowned, untested and no longer matching either the new system's model or the legacy system's model, silently corrupting data in production.

Facade-only ACL: renaming the upstream SDK behind a class without translating its model — the structure of the pattern without its purpose; external types still leak into the domain through the renamed facade.

Using a generic API gateway as the ACL: routing and authentication do not translate domain meanings, so foreign statuses still leak; keep gateway concerns there and put domain-owned translation behind it.

Translating an Open Host Service or Published Language again for no semantic reason: the duplicate mapper drifts from the shared contract and adds incompatible variants; consume the intentionally shared language or document the real local divergence.

Defaulting unknown upstream values to a plausible local value: schema evolution silently changes business meaning and hides drift; reject or represent unknown values explicitly and monitor the mapping failure.

related_patterns_notes.adapter: aligns an interface when semantics already fit; an ACL translates concepts whose meanings differ across bounded contexts.
related_patterns_notes.facade: presents a simpler entry point over one or more operations; it can be part of an ACL but does not by itself protect a model.
related_patterns_notes.gateway: owns transport and access to a remote system; an ACL additionally maps the remote model and failures into local terms.
related_patterns_notes.message-translator: transforms message representations; an ACL uses translation to preserve a downstream context's model across a relationship.
related_patterns_notes.data-transfer-object: carries data across a process or layer; an ACL decides which foreign data becomes a local concept rather than merely carrying fields.
related_patterns_notes.open-host-service: publishes an upstream protocol for many consumers; a downstream that rejects its semantics can place an ACL behind its client.
related_patterns_notes.published-language: supplies a documented shared vocabulary such as FIX; an ACL translates between that language and a context's own model.
related_patterns_notes.separated-domain-model: keeps distinct models within one system boundary; an ACL mediates calls between independently owned models.
related_patterns_notes.strangler-fig: incrementally replaces legacy functionality; an ACL is the translation seam that lets old callers survive each replacement slice.
related_patterns_notes.hexagonal-architecture: organizes dependencies around ports and adapters; an ACL is one concrete boundary adapter protecting a domain model.
related_patterns_notes.ports-and-adapters: makes the domain own the port and infrastructure implement it; an ACL supplies the adapter plus semantic translation at that port.
related_patterns_notes.branch-by-abstraction: switches callers between old and new implementations behind an abstraction; an ACL is needed when the implementations speak different models.
related_patterns_notes.process-manager: coordinates a long-running business transaction; an ACL may translate each participant's messages but does not own transaction policy.
related_patterns_notes.compensating-transaction: reverses an already-applied effect after failure; an ACL may map the provider's reversal API but is not the compensation workflow.
related_patterns_notes.bulkhead: isolates capacity and failure domains; an ACL can sit behind a bulkhead but translation remains its separate responsibility.
related_patterns_notes.retry-with-backoff: retries transient operations with delay; an ACL may classify and apply that policy but must not confuse retries with model translation.
related_patterns_notes.circuit-breaker: stops calls to a failing dependency after repeated errors; an ACL can host the breaker while still translating successes and failures.
